← Back to the case report · CORD Reports
Corrected by a later full static re-analysis. This is CORD's first automated pass, published as produced. Four points below were overturned: the program is a credential-relay shell, not a stealer, and reads nothing from disk; the RCDATA 300 resource is Microsoft's signed WebView2Loader.dll, not a second stage; the window.steamm file bridge is confined to the program's own folder; and the "system fingerprint" at 0x1400094c0 is unreferenced junk that changes size each build. WebView2 is also launched with SmartScreen, Safe Browsing and certificate checks off.

Static analysis · PE32+ · 2026-10-28

Unattributed stealer

MaliciousRole: dropperCapability: stealerFamily: not attributed

This is a 1 MB x64 PE (mingw-linked, no version info, timestamp 2026-09-22) that acts as a WebView2-based credential-phishing lure and dropper. It carries a 164 KB embedded PE in RCDATA resource 300 and drops it to disk at startup. The application creates a frameless browser-control window styled as a login page, bridges JavaScript and native code through a JSON IPC protocol (B10, E19, E20), and collects a system fingerprint using obfuscated XOR/shift arithmetic over PID, tick count and locale (B6, E7). An HTTP client built on WinInet sends requests to two the original file URLs (I1, I2) with 15/30 s timeouts (B3, E3, E4, E14). The lure gives its operator stolen credentials and a machine fingerprint; the dropped PE's purpose is not recovered (U1).

How it runs

The behaviours as a flow, from the entry point: the checks that can end the run, then what it collects, then what it sends and what follows. Boxes follow the order of the analyst's account; a dashed box is code whose path from the entry is not proven. Static analysis: not an observed run.

Throughout: drops embedded PE from resource (B1).

What it does in the full report →

The PE entry (E17) calls a CRT startup that enforces single-instance execution through a LOCK cmpxchg on a global; a second copy spins on Sleep(1000) until the first exits (B8, E9). WinMain (E1) reads its own module path, builds a drop path and writes the RCDATA 300 payload to disk (B1, E2), then loads the WebView2 runtime and creates a centered, DPI-scaled window with DWM extended frame and dark background 0x1f1b1bff (B2, E5). A 1500 ms timer navigates the WebView2 control to a URL (I1) referenced by the setup function at 0x1400056b0.

A JSON IPC protocol bridges WebView2 and native code: a builder at 0x140002900 constructs responses and a parser at 0x1400075c0 dispatches commands (B10, E19, E20). Through this channel the lure page requests file reads (B9, E15), file writes (B9, E16) and URL launches (B5, E6). The UI thread handler (B4, E8) dispatches these in response to JSON messages from the WebView2 frontend.

The HTTP client at 0x140004000 parses URLs with InternetCrackUrlW, opens connections with InternetConnectW, and reads responses with InternetReadFile (B3, E3, E4, E14). Two the original file URLs were recovered (I1, I2); 9 of 11 other URL candidates and all 5 registry-path candidates reside in the embedded PE at file offsets 0xd70c0-0xff420, belonging to unpacked file 1 not the original file (E21, U2, U6). The system fingerprint function at 0x1400094c0 computes a value from PID, tick count and locale through XOR constants 0xfd6c0c64, 0x9c0fc46e, 0x2f77d26c and a shift loop (B6, E7), producing a host identifier sent alongside requests.

What was not recovered: the embedded PE payload's behaviour (U1), the targets of 12 FLOSS decoded strings not mapped to functions (U5), the WebView2 lure content served at runtime (U3), the credential capture mechanism handled by WebView2 JavaScript (U4), the full data set exfiltrated over HTTP (U2), and the purpose of 5 embedded-PE registry paths (U6).

Verdict and detection opportunities all anchor details →

Malicious: a WebView2-based credential-phishing lure that drops an embedded PE at startup, collects a system fingerprint and communicates over HTTP. No family attributed; the cluster label pe/unk.steamlure-28f2b618 agrees with the observed lure behaviour but no family-specific markers were recovered (E13).

Strongest anchors: A1 (entry stub, 30 bytes at file offset 0x400, E17) is a realtime candidate because its rel32 operand varies per binary, making the sequence build-specific; present in 8/8 cluster members. A2 (RCDATA resource 300 containing an embedded PE, E2) is realtime-viable and stable across the cluster. A3 (WinInet HTTP request function with InternetCrackUrl/HttpOpenRequest/HttpSendRequest/InternetReadFile call sequence, E3) is a batch anchor. A4 (system fingerprint function with XOR constants 0xfd6c0c64/0x9c0fc46e/0x2f77d26c, E7) is realtime-viable and distinctive.

Terms used in this report
Original file, unpacked file
The original file is the sample as collected. An unpacked file is one the analysis extracted or decoded from it, numbered in order (in report.json: L0, L1, L2…).
Reachable from the entry point
The static call graph shows a path from where the program starts to this code. It does not mean the code was seen running.
Code present, path not proven
The code is in the file, but the analysis could not prove a route to it, usually because of indirect calls or jump tables.
B, E, A, U, D numbers
Behaviours, evidence items, detection anchors, open questions (unknowns) and derived files (such as decoded strings). Every claim cites the evidence items it rests on.
API hashing
Looking up Windows functions at run time by a hash of their name, so the names never appear in the file.
MBA
Mixed boolean-arithmetic: computing a simple constant through a tangle of AND, OR, XOR and arithmetic.
ATT&CK, MBC
Public catalogues of attacker techniques (MITRE ATT&CK) and malware behaviours (MBC).
IOC
Indicator of compromise: a value, such as a domain or file name, that shows up on an infected host or network.

U4

Q2

what was tried
read navigation event handler 0x140008f60 and URL handler 0x140003c10; neither shows explicit credential extraction in the original file, deepen: identified JSON IPC protocol (0x140002900 builder, 0x1400075c0 parser); ui_thread_handler 0x140005a90 dispatches to file_reader/file_writer/url_launcher/WndProc via JSON messages from WebView2 frontend

credential capture handled by WebView2 JavaScript sending postMessage to native code; the native handlers (file_reader, file_writer, url_launcher) execute commands but extraction logic is in the lure page served to WebView2
